Field studies of the Yellow Irish lord (Hemilepidotus jordani) have documented that newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge at a remarkably small size, with wet weight at birth estimated at 0.0023 grams [Wwb = 0.0023 grams]. This minute mass, which reflects the modest egg diameter characteristic of many cottid fishes, imposes a stringent energetic constraint on the lecithotrophic phase; the prolarva must complete mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding before its endogenous yolk reserves are exhausted. Following the exotrophic transition, juvenile growth proceeds steadily, and individuals recruit to the benthic habitat at a size that permits them to exploit the amphipod and decapod prey typical of nearshore rocky substrates. As these juveniles enter the sub-adult phase, their growth trajectory begins to decelerate, and published length-at-age data suggest that total length at puberty is approximately 36 centimeters [Lp = approximately 36 centimeters], a developmental milestone that marks the onset of gametogenesis and the individual's transition to a reproductively viable organism.

At the prevailing bottom temperatures of the northern Pacific continental shelf, which average 3.5 °C [T = 3.5 °C], female Yellow Irish lord achieve a maximum reproductive output that is notable among medium-bodied sculpins. The annual fecundity, when estimated from relative fecundity data of 266 eggs per gram of somatic mass, yields a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 615 eggs per day, which translates to an annual output of approximately 224,508 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 224,508 eggs per year]. This high fecundity is a classic bet-hedging strategy typical of cold-water cottids, compensating for the elevated mortality risk faced by the small, planktonic early life stages. The protracted spawning season that accompanies this output is presumably facilitated by the stable, low-temperature regime, which slows metabolic turnover and allows females to sustain vitellogenesis over many weeks, thereby buffering the population against interannual variability in food supply during the critical larval drift period.

The ultimate total length attained by Hemilepidotus jordani has been recorded at 65 centimeters [Li = 65 centimeters], a size that places this species among the larger members of the genus. Achieving this maximum known length requires sustained growth over many years; length-weight regressions fitted to local field samples indicate that an individual of 65 centimeters in length carries an ultimate wet weight of approximately 3,800 grams [Wwi = approximately 3,800 grams]. This substantial body mass is associated with a shift in trophic ecology, as large adults are capable of handling sizeable crabs and even small demersal fishes, whereas smaller conspecifics remain confined to foraging on gammarid amphipods. The energetic demands of attaining such a large size are considerable, and growth curves derived from otolith increment analyses suggest that the annual growth increment declines sharply after the onset of sexual maturity, with resources increasingly diverted toward gonadal investment rather than somatic expansion during the later years of life.

In the cold, thermally stable waters of the Gulf of Alaska and the Bering Sea, where temperatures consistently hover near 3.5 °C [T = 3.5 °C], the maximum lifespan of the Yellow Irish lord has been estimated at approximately 30 years [am = approximately 30 years]. This remarkable longevity for a demersal cottid is almost certainly linked to the depressed metabolic rates imposed by the near-freezing ambient conditions; the Arrhenius effect on somatic maintenance costs means that individuals living at 3.5 °C experience a markedly slower rate of physiological aging compared to conspecifics in warmer, more southerly portions of the range. The trade-off, however, is a delayed reproductive schedule: females typically attain a wet weight at puberty of about 580 grams [Wwp = about 580 grams], a mass that is reached only after several years of steady, slow growth. This combination of late maturity, moderate fecundity, and very long reproductive lifespan aligns the species with a classic slow life-history strategy, well suited to the high-latitude environments where food availability is seasonal but adult mortality from predation is relatively low.

Comparative morphometric analyses of Hemilepidotus jordani demonstrate that the length-weight relationship derived from field specimens (based on the equation 0.00676 times length raised to the 3.17 power) yields internally consistent predictions across the life cycle. For instance, the computed ultimate wet mass of 3,800 grams [Wwi = 3,800 grams] for a 65-centimeter (65 centimeters) [Li = 65 centimeters] fish is matched by a corresponding pubertal body mass of 580 grams [Wwp = 580 grams] for an individual at 36 centimeters [Lp = 36 centimeters] total length. This allometric scaling suggests that body shape and condition remain relatively uniform throughout the adult phase, a finding corroborated by field measurements of the condition factor across seasons. The long-term monitoring programs that produced these data have also confirmed that the average water temperature experienced by this species throughout its benthic existence is 3.5 °C [T = 3.5 °C], a value that profoundly influences every aspect of its bioenergetics, from the larval yolk absorption rate to the senescence schedule that ultimately limits lifespan to 30 years [am = 30 years] in the wild.

Continuing the life history description, the reproductive schedule of this species is further shaped by the interplay between body size accumulation and the cold thermal environment. The wet weight at birth of 0.0023 grams [Wwb = 0.0023 grams] represents the smallest stage in an ontogenetic trajectory that spans nearly six orders of magnitude to the adult mass. Experimental rearing studies under controlled conditions at 3.5 °C [T = 3.5 °C] have shown that the yolk-sac larvae begin exogenous feeding within a few weeks after eclosion, marking a critical transition from lecithotrophy to planktivory. The protracted juvenile phase, which lasts several years before the attainment of puberty at 36 centimeters [Lp = 36 centimeters] and 580 grams [Wwp = 580 grams], reflects the slow growth rates imposed by the cold, food-limited environment of the continental shelf. This extended pre-reproductive period is a common feature among long-lived boreal fishes and is thought to enhance lifetime reproductive success by allowing individuals to reach a sufficiently large body size to produce large, high-quality clutches when they finally mature.
